name: Cetylpyridinium chloride mouthwash
lead: Cetylpyridinium chloride (CPC) mouthwash is an over-the-counter antiseptic rinse built around a quaternary ammonium compound that kills bacteria and disrupts the membranes of enveloped viruses.[11] Typical products contain about 0.05 percent CPC and are sold for plaque, gingivitis and bad breath.[7]

Reviews report a small but significant added benefit on plaque and gingivitis when CPC rinses are used with toothbrushing, generally less than chlorhexidine.[11][12] Tooth staining and temporary taste changes are reported side effects.[11] During the COVID-19 pandemic, CPC rinses were also trialled for reducing SARS-CoV-2 in saliva.[2][5]
infobox: Oral rinse, also in lozenges and sprays[11]

paras: CPC is used in mouthwashes, toothpastes, lozenges and throat sprays.[11] Randomised trials have compared 0.05 percent CPC rinse with 0.12 percent chlorhexidine for plaque and gingival inflammation, and with tea tree oil rinses in a short plaque regrowth model.[3][7] A 2025 double-blind trial examined CPC rinse on halitosis and tongue microbiota in people in orthodontic treatment.[10]

Wikipedia and its cited reviews describe CPC as adding a small benefit to brushing for plaque and gingivitis.[11] A 1997 six-week double-blind study of 129 people examined effects on normal oral flora and on colonisation by non-oral species.[4] An in vitro study compared 0.05 percent chlorhexidine and 0.05 percent CPC against bacteria in biofilms, and another trial examined rinses before dental implant surgery and toothbrush disinfection.[6][8][9]

Tooth staining is reported in about 3 percent of users, and a small percentage notice temporary taste alteration that resolves after stopping. Concentrated solutions irritate mucous membranes.[11] Procter and Gamble faced a 2009 class action over staining from a CPC rinse, which was dismissed in 2010.[11]

A double-blind randomised trial in SARS-CoV-2 positive outpatients assessed CPC rinses on viral shedding, and a 2023 systematic review of randomised trials reviewed efficacy against the virus.[2][5] A lipidomics study found oral rinses disrupt the viral envelope in vivo.[1] Plaque and gingivitis trials versus chlorhexidine and tea tree oil are listed above.[3][7]

timeline.event: A CPC-based rinse launches in the US market.[11]
Class-action suit over tooth staining filed; dismissed in 2010.[11]
Randomised trial of CPC rinses on SARS-CoV-2 shedding published.[2]

card.summary: The standard drugstore antibacterial rinse; modest added plaque benefit, weaker than chlorhexidine, with some staining.
card.note: Tooth staining in a small share of users; temporary taste changes reported.

quick.overview:
CPC mouthwash is the common over-the-counter antibacterial rinse, usually at about 0.05 percent. Reviews describe a small added benefit over brushing alone for plaque and gum inflammation.

It also drew research interest during COVID-19 because it breaks down the lipid coat of some viruses.
quick.mechanism: CPC is a positively charged quaternary ammonium compound that binds to and disrupts bacterial and viral membranes.
quick.risks: Tooth staining is reported in roughly 3 percent of users and taste alteration is usually temporary. The US FDA monograph covers short-term OTC use at 0.025 to 0.1 percent.
